findings.claim: The brief says that Corollary 1.6.1 is equivalent to Theorem 1.2.1. It is only a corollary, and the converse does not hold. Closed-surface groups are not free. For n ≥ 1, Mod_{g,n}-finiteness is much weaker than Out(F_{2g+n−1})-finiteness, since Mod_{g,n} preserves peripheral conjugacy classes. For example, an infinite-order character of π₁(Σ_{0,4}) = F₃ is PMod_{0,4}-invariant but has infinite Out(F₃)-orbit. A design job that states the final theorems as equivalent could plan a nonexistent reduction.

findings.claim: Item 34 copies a misprint of Theorem 4.2.1: it says H⁰(X, W) carries 'a natural real Hodge structure'. As written this reads as a pure Hodge structure, and the statement is then false. W is a variation of mixed Hodge structure, and the fixed part carries a real mixed Hodge structure. Take W constant with a mixed Hodge structure that has two different weights. Then H⁰ = W, and the inclusion cannot be a morphism of mixed Hodge structures from any pure structure, because morphisms of MHS are strict for W: the image would meet W_{k-1} trivially, but here it does not. The paper itself uses the mixed version. No sourceIssue records the misprint.

Proof of Proposition 4.2.2, same page: 'By the theorem of the fixed part, Theorem 4.2.1, Q carries a canonical real mixed Hodge structure such that the evaluation map Q ⊗ L̃ → W is a map of variations'. The TeX source reads 'natural real Hodge structure' too.

Without them the theorem of the fixed part (item 34) cannot be applied to L̃^∨ ⊗ W. No item states either fact. Item 30 only defines admissibility, and the note of item 36 does not mention the step. findings.claim: The proof of Lemma 4.3.2 uses three external results that have no items. (1) [Moc06, Lemma 10.13] deforms a G(ℂ)-valued representation, with G the reductive Zariski closure, to one underlying a PVHS. This is a different cited result from [Moc06, Theorem 10.5] (item 37), and item 38 mentions it only in its note. (2) Weil's infinitesimal rigidity: H¹(π₁, 𝔤) = 0 implies that the conjugation orbit of ρ is open in Hom(π₁, G), which is what 'ρ is rigid and hence admits no non-trivial deformations' means. To conclude ρ = ρ₀ the orbit must also be closed, which needs the G-valued analogue of item 71 (item 71 is stated only for GL_r). (3) The Zariski closure of the image of a semisimple representation is reductive. PROTOCOL §16 requires each cited result to be an item.
findings.evidence: arXiv v4, proof of Lemma 4.3.2, p. 27: 'Let G denote the Zariski-closure of the image of ρ. Note G is reductive by semisimplicity of ρ. ... Hence ρ is cohomologically rigid as a G-representation, as H1(X, g) ⊂ H1(X, ad ρ) = 0. We may apply [Moc06, Lemma 10.13], which yields that ρ admits a deformation as a G(C)-representation to ρ0 : π1(X) → G(C), which underlies a PVHS. But ρ is rigid and hence admits no non-trivial deformations. This implies ρ = ρ0'. A search of all 139 item statements for 'Weil', 'local rigidity', 'open orbit' and 'Lemma 10.13' finds the last only in the notes of items 38 and the Moc06 prerequisite.
findings.fix: Add items, status missing, routed to HodgeStructuresPartII. findings.claim: Item 37 (Mochizuki's Theorem 4.3.1) says only that rho 'admits a deformation with constant determinant to a representation underlying a complex PVHS'. Neither the paper nor the extraction defines a deformation over anything but an Artin local C-algebra. The consumer, Theorem 8.5.3 (item 69), goes through Lemma 8.5.2 (item 68). That lemma needs a family rho: pi_1(C°) -> GL_r(O_X(X)) over a connected finite-type C-scheme X with constant determinant, with one closed point at V and one at V_0. Read with the paper's only definitions (§3.1), Theorem 4.3.1 does not even parse: an Artinian deformation cannot reach a different PVHS point. 'Constant determinant' over O_X(X) is also undefined. As extracted, item 37 is a target that cannot be formalised and does not compose with item 68. The paper has this gap and it is not among E1-E22.
findings.evidence: Theorem 4.3.1, p. 27: 'Any representation ρ: π1(X) → GLr(C) with finite determinant admits a deformation with constant determinant to a representation underlying a complex PVHS.' §3.1, p. 20, the only definition: 'Let Art be the category of local Artin C-algebras with residue field C. If A ∈ Art ... we say that a representation ρA: G → GLr(A) is a deformation of ρ0 if ρA = ρ0 mod mA ... Say a deformation ρA of ρ0 has constant determinant if det ρA = det ρ0'. Lemma 8.5.2, p. 42: 'Let X be a finite-type connected C-scheme, and let ρ: π1(C°, c) → GLr(OX(X)) be a representation with r < √(g+1) and constant determinant.' Proof of Theorem 8.5.3, p. 43: 'By Theorem 4.3.1, V admits a deformation with constant determinant to a local system V0 underlying a complex PVHS ... To conclude, it's enough to show that V|C° = V0|C°. But this is immediate from Lemma 8.5.2.' Item 111 (planned R04.1/R04.2) and item 26 cover deformations over Artin rings only. No item defines a family of representations over a finite-type base.
findings.fix: Restate item 37 in the form item 68 consumes. findings.claim: Example 10.1.6(2) claims that for every n > 0 the sequence 0 → I²/I³ → I/I³ → I/I² → 0 of PMod_{g,n}-modules does not split. Item 85 copies this. It is false for (g,n) = (1,1) and (0,3), both allowed by the paper's standing hyperbolicity convention (Notation 1.10.1). (1,1): PMod_{1,1} ≅ SL₂(ℤ) acts on π₁(Σ_{1,0}, x) = ℤ² through SL₂(ℤ). The central element −I induces an involution of I/I³ acting by (−1)^k on I^k/I^{k+1}. Its (−1)-eigenspace is SL₂(ℤ)-stable, meets I²/I³ trivially and maps onto I/I², so it splits the sequence. (0,3): PMod_{0,3} is trivial, so every extension splits. The sequence does not split when π₁(Σ_{g,n−1}) is non-abelian: the point-pushing subgroup acts on I/I³ through h−1 ↦ (h−1) + [γ−1, h−1], and this action is non-trivial although it is trivial on both graded pieces. For the same reason, part (1) needs g ≥ 3, since ∧³H/H = 0 for g = 2 because x ↦ x∧ω is an isomorphism H → ∧³H. Part (3) needs g ≥ 2, since H¹(SL₂(ℤ), ℚ²) = 0 because −I acts by −1.
findings.evidence: Example 10.1.6(2), p. 51: 'For n > 0 the group PMod_{g,n} acts on π1(Σ_{g,n−1}, x) … Then direct computation shows that the short exact sequence of PMod_{g,n}-representations 0 → I²/I³ → I/I³ → I/I² → 0 does not split'. Notation 1.10.1, p. 10: 'We fix non-negative integers (g,n) so that n ≥ 1 if g = 1 and n ≥ 3 if g = 0'.
findings.fix: In item 85 add the hypotheses: (1) g ≥ 3; (2) n > 0 and Σ_{g,n−1} hyperbolic, i.e. 2g + n − 3 > 0; (3) g ≥ 2. Add a sourceIssue (error, Example 10.1.6(2), p. 51, affects nothing), with the (1,1) counterexample given here.

findings.claim: Item 131 states [LL22, Lemma 7.5.1] for any n-punctured genus g surface and r > 1: finite-image representations are not Zariski-dense in the character variety. Without hyperbolicity this is false. For Σ_{1,0} (π₁ = ℤ²) and r = 2, the semisimple character variety is Sym²((ℂ^×)²). Finite-image points are pairs of torsion characters, which are Zariski-dense; the commutator relation of the proof holds identically because π₁ is abelian. Likewise for π₁ = ℤ or 1. LL22's standing convention is that curves are hyperbolic, and this paper's Notation 1.10.1 imposes the same convention. Item 77 (Theorem 9.1.2) also omits hyperbolicity, without which M_{g,n} is not a Deligne–Mumford stack.

findings.claim: Item 136 applies Voisin's harmonic theory with 'F = ℰ ⊗ Ω¹_𝒞(log 𝒟) with the metric from the unitary structure'. The flat unitary metric on V ⊗ O_{𝒞°} does not extend to a smooth hermitian metric on the Deligne canonical extension ℰ when the local monodromy is non-trivial. Unitarity enters elsewhere, through the constancy of b ↦ h⁰(𝒞_b, ℰ_b ⊗ Ω¹(log 𝒟_b)), that is, the local freeness of F¹ℋ in (5.1), which uses Timmerscheidt's degeneration. findings.claim: This is an unrecorded gap in the paper. Theorem 1.2.1 is stated 'for g, n, r ≥ 0', but its proof goes through Theorem 8.5.3, whose first step is Corollary 2.3.5: a punctured versal family over a dominant étale ℳ → M_{g,n}. That construction exists only under Notation 1.10.1's hyperbolicity. So the non-hyperbolic case (g, n) = (1, 0), where r < √2 forces r = 1, is not covered as written. (For g = 0 the bound gives r = 0.) The case does follow from Proposition 2.3.1, which is stated for g ≥ 1 and n ≥ 0. The paper uses exactly this shortcut in Proposition 8.4.1 but not in Theorem 8.5.3. Also: Theorem 1.2.1 is stated for all g, n ≥ 0, and Theorem 8.5.3 carries no hyperbolicity hypothesis. Yet the proof of Theorem 8.5.3 begins with Corollary 2.3.5 (a punctured versal family) and then uses [LL22, Theorem 1.2.12]. Both require Notation 1.10.1, which fixes (g, n) hyperbolic. The only non-hyperbolic case with r ≥ 1 is (g, n) = (1, 0). There r < √2 forces r = 1, and Proposition 2.3.1 (g ≥ 1, n ≥ 0) settles it, but §8.5 never routes it there. Proposition 8.4.1 does route its low-genus case there ('If g < 3, r ≤ 1').
findings.evidence: Theorem 1.2.1, p. 3: 'For g, n, r ≥ 0, let ρ : π₁(Σ_{g,n}) → GL_r(ℂ) be a MCG-finite representation. If r < √(g+1), then ρ has finite image.' Proof of Theorem 8.5.3, p. 43: 'By Corollary 2.3.5, there exists a dominant étale map ℳ → M_{g,n}…'. Proof of Proposition 8.4.1, p. 41: 'If g < 3, r ≤ 1, and so we may conclude by Proposition 2.3.1.' Call such a family versal if the induced map M → Mg,n is dominant and étale.' Proof of Theorem 8.5.3, p. 43: 'By Corollary 2.3.5, there exists a dominant étale map M → Mg,n ...'. Corollary 2.3.5, p. 18, assumes only 'g ≥ 1'. Proposition 2.3.1, p. 15: 'Let g ≥ 1, n ≥ 0. Then any MCG-finite representation ρ: π1(Σg,n) → C^× has finite image.'

findings.claim: This is an unrecorded gap in the proof of Proposition 2.3.4. The proof passes to one dominant étale base change that kills every element of E₂^{2,0} and E₂^{1,1} of the old base, and concludes that every element of ker η dies. That inference fails. Killing the image of ε(ρ̃) in E^{1,1} only moves ε(ρ̃)|_{ℳ′} into F² = im(H²(π₁(ℳ′), μ) → H²(π₁(𝒞′°), μ)). There it equals the inflation of a class z′ ∈ H²(π₁(ℳ′), μ), and z′ need not be pulled back from H²(π₁(ℳ), μ), so killing the old E₂^{2,0} does not kill it. A filtered map that vanishes on both graded pieces need not vanish. The fix is a second application of Lemma 2.3.3.

findings.claim: Item 12's note says Proposition 2.1.1 'is what allows the induction on the socle filtration in §8.7: both the socle and the quotient by it are MCG-finite'. Proposition 2.1.1 gives MCG-finiteness only for semisimple subquotients, and ρ/soc ρ is in general not semisimple. The quotient is MCG-finite for a different reason: soc(ρ∘γ) = soc(ρ) as subspaces, so every isomorphism ρ∘γ ≅ ρ preserves the socle. Item 126 states that reason correctly.

Item 126: 'For an automorphism γ of G, soc(ρ ∘ γ) = soc(ρ) as subspaces. Hence if ρ is MCG-finite, so are soc(ρ) and ρ/soc(ρ).'
findings.fix: In item 12's note, replace the sentence with: 'It gives MCG-finiteness of soc(ρ). The MCG-finiteness of ρ/soc(ρ), which is not semisimple in general, is the separate fact in item 126.' Make item 2's dependency list cite item 126 for the inductive step.

findings.claim: Item 89, copying Notation A.1.2, says '(A^•_{log D}(ℰ), ∇ + ∂̄) is the de Rham resolution of the unitary local system V'. The complex lives on the compact total space 𝒞, while V lives only on 𝒞°. For the canonical extension, the complex resolves Rj_*V (Deligne's logarithmic comparison), and that is what makes its relative hypercohomology equal to ℋ = R¹π°_*V ⊗ O.
